en: Parivāra 7.
Ekuttarikanaya 1. Ekakavāra (The Singlefold Chapter)
The things that cause an offense should be known.
The things that do not cause an offense should be known.
The offense itself should be known.
A non-offense is to be known.
A light offense is to be known.
A grave offense is to be known.
An offense with remainder should be known.
An offense without remainder should be known.
A grave offense should be known.
An offense that is not grave should be known.
An offense that can be remedied should be known.
An offense that cannot be remedied should be known.
An offense that requires confession should be known.
An offense that does not require confession should be known.
An obstructive offense should be known.
An offense that constitutes an obstacle must be known.
An offense defined as blameworthy must be known.
An offense defined as blameless must be known.
An offense arising from action should be known.
An offense arising from non-action should be known.
An offense arising from both action and non-action should be known.
The prior offense should be known.
The subsequent offense should be known.
The intermediate offense between prior offenses should be known.
An intermediate offense among other offenses is to be known.
An offense that, once confessed, counts toward the formal tally is to be known.
An offense that, though confessed, does not count toward the formal tally is to be known.
The original formulation (paññatti) is to be known.
The supplementary formulation (anupaññatti) is to be known.
The yet-to-be-enacted formulation (anuppannapaññatti) is to be known.
The universal formulation should be known.
The partial formulation should be known.
The common formulation should be known.
The uncommon designation (asādhāraṇapaññatti) should be known.
The one-sided designation (ekatopaññatti) should be known.
The twofold designation (ubhatopaññatti) should be known.
An offense of grave censure is to be known.
An offense not of grave censure is to be known.
An offense connected with householders is to be known.
An offense connected with householders should be known.
A fixed offense should be known.
An unfixed offense should be known.
The person who is an originator should be known.
The person who is not an originator should be known.
The person who commits an offense occasionally should be known.
The person who repeatedly commits offenses should be known.
The person who reproves should be known.
The person who is reproved should be known.
The person who reproves unrighteously is to be known;
the person who is reproved unrighteously is to be known;
the person who reproves righteously is to be known.
A person who has been reproved by the Dhamma should be known;
a person who is fixed in destiny should be known;
a person who is not fixed in destiny should be known.
A person incapable of committing an offense is to be known.
A person capable of committing an offense is to be known.
A person who has been suspended is to be known.
A person who has been suspended should be known.
A person who has been expelled should be known.
A person who has not been expelled should be known.
A person who belongs to the same community should be known;
a person who does not belong to the same community should be known;
and the setting aside [of a person] should be known.
The section on single [offenses] is finished.
Its summary verse:
"Actions, offenses, and light [penalties]."
And there is the grave offense with remainder;
confession through remedial action,
and the commission of a fault in the interval.
The functional and non-functional are first;
those that fall within the count are intermediate;
the designation is for what has not yet arisen.
And those common to all [monks] together;
the state of being a wife in a large household, and so forth; one who accuses without cause;
One who is fixed in what is non-Dhamma,
one incapable [of rehabilitation], one who has been cast out, one who has been expelled, and the setting aside of one who is equal [to the Saṅgha].
The summary verse: "In the section on single items, 'this'.
2. The Section on Pairs:
There is an offense that is a liberation through perception; there is an offense that is not a liberation through perception.
There is an offense for one who has attained meditative absorption; there is an offense for one who has not attained meditative absorption.
There is an offense connected with the true Dhamma; there is an offense connected with what is not the true Dhamma.
There is an offense connected with one’s own requisites; there is an offense connected with another’s requisites.
There is an offense connected with one’s own person; there is an offense connected with another person.
There is the case where one who speaks the truth incurs a heavy offense, while one who speaks falsehood incurs a light offense.
There is the case where one who speaks falsehood incurs a heavy offense, while one who speaks the truth incurs a light offense.
There is an offense that one commits when on the ground, not when in the air.
There is an offense that one commits when in the air, not when on the ground.
There is an offense that one commits when going out, not when entering.
There is an offense that one incurs when entering, but not when departing.
There is an offense that one incurs by undertaking [a practice], and there is an offense that one incurs by not undertaking it.
There is an offense that one incurs by formally undertaking [a precept], and there is an offense that one incurs by not formally undertaking it.
There is an offense that one incurs by committing; there is an offense that one incurs without committing.
There is an offense that one incurs by giving; there is an offense that one incurs without giving.
There is an offense that one incurs by confessing; there is an offense that one incurs without confessing.
There is an offense incurred by accepting; there is an offense not incurred by accepting.
There is an offense incurred through use; there is an offense not incurred through use.
There is an offense incurred at night, not by day.
There is an offense one incurs by day, but not by night.
There is an offense one incurs at sunrise, and there is an offense one does not incur at sunrise.
There is an offense one incurs while cutting, and there is an offense one incurs while not cutting.
There is an offense committed by one who conceals another's offense; there is an offense committed by one who does not conceal another's offense.
There is an offense committed by one who remembers another's offense; there is an offense committed by one who does not remember another's offense.
There are two Uposatha days.
The fourteenth-day [Uposatha] and the fifteenth-day [Uposatha].
There are two Pavāraṇās—
the fourteenth-day and the fifteenth-day.
There are two kinds of formal acts:
a formal act by announcement and a formal act by resolution.
There are another two kinds of formal acts as well:
A formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation; a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations.
There are two bases for formal acts:
the basis for a formal act consisting of a mere intimation, and the basis for a formal act consisting of a motion.
There are two other bases for legal acts:
the basis for a legal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation, and the basis for a legal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations.
There are two defects of legal acts:
The fault of a *apalokana* (informal) procedure, the fault of a *ñatti* (motion) procedure.
Furthermore, there are two other faults of procedures:
the fault of a *ñattidutiyakamma* (procedure with one motion and one proclamation), and the fault of a *ñatticatutthakamma* (procedure with one motion and three proclamations).
There are two kinds of success in formal acts:
success in a formal act by announcement, and success in a formal act by resolution.
There are another two kinds of success in formal acts:
The success of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second; the success of a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth.
There are two grounds for being of a different communion:
either one makes oneself of a different communion, or a united Saṅgha suspends one for not seeing [the offense], for not making amends, or for not relinquishing [the wrong view].
There are two grounds for being of common affiliation:

either one makes oneself of common affiliation with oneself, or a united Saṅgha reinstates one who has been suspended, whether for not seeing [an offense], for not making amends, or for not relinquishing [a wrong view].
There are two rules involving defeat (pārājika).
For both monks and nuns: two *saṅghādisesa* offenses,
two *thullaccaya* offenses, two *pācittiya* offenses, two *pāṭidesanīya* offenses, two *dukkaṭa* offenses, and two *dubbhāsita* offenses—
for both monks and nuns.
There are seven offenses, seven classes of offenses.
The Saṅgha is split in two ways:
either by formal act or by the drawing of lots.
Two persons should not be ordained:
one deficient in age and one deficient in limbs.
Furthermore, two other persons should not be ordained:
One who has failed in the basis, and one who commits an offense of wrong-doing through the formal act.
Furthermore, there are two other persons who should not be ordained:
one who is incomplete and one who, though complete, does not request ordination.
One should not live in dependence upon two kinds of persons:
one who is shameless and one who is foolish. One should not grant dependence to two kinds of persons: [one who is shameless and one who is foolish].
One who is shameless does not ask for support from one who is conscientious.
Support should be given to two types of persons:
to the fool who is conscientious and to the one who asks.
Two persons are incapable of committing an offense:
Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas.
Two persons are capable of committing an offense: [all others].
Bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs.
Two persons are incapable of intentionally committing an offense:
bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs who are noble persons (ariyapuggala).
Two types of persons are capable of intentionally committing an offense:
bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs who are worldlings (puthujjana).
Two types of persons are incapable of intentionally transgressing a matter that involves an excess: [the arahants].
Bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs are noble persons (ariyapuggala).
Two types of persons are capable of intentionally committing an offense that exceeds the limit:
bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs who are worldlings (puthujjana).
There are two ways of protesting:
one protests either by body or by speech.
There are two ways of bringing about removal:
There is a person who has not reached the point of being rehabilitated; if the Saṅgha rehabilitates him, in one case he is properly rehabilitated, and in another case he is improperly rehabilitated.
There are two kinds of rehabilitation:
there is a person who has not reached the point of being rehabilitated; if the Saṅgha rehabilitates him, in one case he is rightly rehabilitated, and in another case he is wrongly rehabilitated.
There are two kinds of acknowledgment:
one acknowledges by means of the body, or one acknowledges by means of speech.
There are two kinds of acceptance:
One receives with the body or receives with what is attached to the body.
There are two ways of declining:
one declines with the body or one declines with speech.
There are two kinds of harm:
harm to the training and harm to one's livelihood.
There are two kinds of censure:
He reproves either by body or by speech.
There are two impediments to the kaṭhina:
the impediment of the residence and the impediment of the robe-cloth.
There are two non-obstructions to the kaṭhina:
the non-obstruction of the residence and the non-obstruction of the robe.
There are two robes:
There are two kinds of robes: those from householders and rag-robes.
There are two kinds of bowls:
iron bowls and clay bowls.
There are two kinds of bowls:
those made of tin and those made of lead.
There are two ways of determining the size of a bowl.
One either resolves it by means of the body or one resolves it by means of speech.
There are two ways of resolving a robe:
one resolves it by means of the body or one resolves it by means of speech.
There are two kinds of assignment:
assignment in the presence and assignment in the absence.
There are two kinds of discipline:
Of monks and of nuns. There are two types of Vinaya-experts:
those who know the formulated rules and those who know what is in conformity with the formulated rules.
There are two ways of effacing the taints in the Vinaya:
the demolition of the bridge over what is unallowable, and moderation in what is allowable.
One incurs an offense in two ways:
One commits an offense either by means of the body or by means of speech.
One emerges from the offense in two ways:
one emerges either by means of the body or by means of speech.
There are two types of probation:
probation for concealed offenses and probation for unconcealed offenses.
There are another two types of probation:
The probation for the end of purity and the probation for reconciliation.
There are two types of *mānatta*:
*mānatta* for concealed offenses and *mānatta* for unconcealed offenses.
There are two other types of *mānatta*:
the *pakkhamānatta* (the *mānatta* for a fortnight) and the *samodhānamānatta* (the *mānatta* by combination).
For two kinds of persons, there is a breaking of the continuity of the nights.
For one who is undergoing probation and for one who is practicing the *mānatta* penance.
There are two types of disrespect:
disrespect for persons and disrespect for the Dhamma.
There are two kinds of salt:
natural and prepared. There are also another two kinds of salt: [natural and prepared].
Sea salt and black salt.
There are two other salts as well:
rock salt and earth-born salt.
There are also two other types of salt:
sea salt and rock salt.
There are two kinds of enjoyment:
There is internal enjoyment and external enjoyment.
There are two kinds of abuse: base abuse and exalted abuse.
Slander occurs in two ways:
either by one who desires favor or by one who intends to cause a schism.
Group-meals are produced in two ways:
Either by invitation or by request.
There are two periods for entering the rains residence: the earlier and the later.
There are two ways of suspending the Pātimokkha that are contrary to the Dhamma;
there are two ways of suspending the Pātimokkha that are in accordance with the Dhamma.
There are two types of persons who are foolish:
There are two types of persons who carry the burden that has not yet come: the one who carries the future burden and the one who does not carry the burden that has already arrived.
There are two types of wise persons:
the one who does not carry the future burden and the one who carries the burden that has already arrived.
Furthermore, there are two other types of foolish persons:

one who perceives what is unallowable as allowable, and one who perceives what is allowable as unallowable. There are two types of wise persons: [one who perceives what is unallowable as unallowable, and one who perceives what is allowable as allowable].
One who perceives what is improper as improper, and one who perceives what is proper as proper.
There are also two other types of fools:
one who perceives what is not an offense as an offense, and one who perceives what is an offense as not an offense.
Two persons are wise:

he who perceives an offense as an offense, and he who perceives what is not an offense as not an offense. Furthermore, two other persons are fools: [he who perceives an offense as not an offense, and he who perceives what is not an offense as an offense].
One who perceives what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and one who perceives what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma.
Two persons are wise:
one who perceives what is non-Dhamma as non-Dhamma, and one who perceives what is Dhamma as Dhamma.
Furthermore, there are two other types of foolish persons:

one who perceives what is not the discipline as the discipline, and one who perceives the discipline as not the discipline. There are two types of wise persons: [one who perceives what is not the discipline as not the discipline, and one who perceives the discipline as the discipline].

He who perceives what is not in accordance with the discipline as not being in accordance with the discipline, and he who perceives what is in accordance with the discipline as being in accordance with the discipline—
for these two persons, the taints increase:
he who feels remorse for what should not be felt as remorse, and he who does not feel remorse for what should be felt as remorse.
The taints do not increase for two types of persons:

one who does not feel remorse about what is not to be regretted, and one who feels remorse about what is to be regretted. Furthermore, the taints increase for another two types of persons: [one who feels remorse about what is not to be regretted, and one who does not feel remorse about what is to be regretted].
One who perceives what is improper as proper, and one who perceives what is proper as improper—
in these two persons, the taints do not increase.
But for one who perceives what is improper as improper, and for one who perceives what is proper as proper, the taints do not increase.
The taints increase for two other types of persons:

one who perceives what is not an offense as an offense, and one who perceives what is an offense as not an offense. The taints do not increase for two types of persons: [one who perceives what is not an offense as not an offense, and one who perceives what is an offense as an offense].
One who perceives what is not an offense as not an offense, and one who perceives what is an offense as an offense.
Furthermore, the taints increase for two other types of persons:
one who perceives what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and one who perceives what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma.
The taints do not increase for two types of persons:

one who perceives what is non-Dhamma as non-Dhamma, and one who perceives what is Dhamma as Dhamma. Furthermore, the taints increase for another two types of persons: [one who perceives what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and one who perceives what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma].

One who perceives what is not in accordance with the discipline as being in accordance with the discipline, and one who perceives what is in accordance with the discipline as not being in accordance with the discipline—
for these two persons, the taints do not increase.

But for one who perceives what is not in accordance with the discipline as not being in accordance with the discipline, and for one who perceives what is in accordance with the discipline as being in accordance with the discipline, the taints do not increase.
The pairs are finished.
Its summary verse:
Perception, attainment, and the true Dhamma.
Requisites and persons;
truth, the ground, departing,
taking up, and undertaking.
Doing, giving, and taking,
by means of enjoyment and night;
at dawn, cutting, and covering.
And while observing the Uposatha,
there are other formal acts of invitation (pavāraṇā), other legal procedures (kamma),
other bases (vatthu), and faults (dosa).
There are two other attainments:
the diverse and the identical.
[The offenses are] pārājika, saṅghādisesa, thullaccaya, and so forth.
The Pācittis and the Pāṭidesanīyas;
the Dukkaṭas and the Dubbhāsitas,
and the seven classes of offenses (āpattikkhandha).
The full ordination is broken,
and likewise two others;
one should neither dwell [with them] nor grant [ordination].
Incapable and capable,
intentional, and with transgression;
protestation, and formal dismissal.
Reinstatement and admission,
acceptance and rejection;
The harmful and the admonition.
And likewise two kinds of Kathina;
robes, bowls, and circular cloths,
as well as two kinds of formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna).
The formal assignment according to the Vinaya,
the discipline, and the effacement;
one incurs an offense and emerges from it.
Two further [cases] regarding the parivāsa;
two further regarding the mānatta;
and the interruption of the night and disrespect.
Two on salt, three others,
and the abuse of use;
slander and [taking] from a group.
"Setting aside" refers to what is permissible as a burden;
there is no offense regarding that which is non-Dhamma as Dhamma,
or likewise regarding taints in the Vinaya.
3. The Section on Triads:
There is an offense committed while the Blessed One is still living, but not when he has attained final Nibbāna;
there is an offense committed when the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, but not while he is still living.
There is an offense that one commits both while the Blessed One is present and when he has attained final nibbāna.
There is an offense that one commits at the proper time, not at an improper time;
there is an offense that one commits at an improper time, not at the proper time.
There is an offense that one commits both at the proper time and at the improper time.
There is an offense that one commits by night, not by day;
there is an offense that one commits by day, not by night.
There is an offense that one incurs both by night and by day.
There is an offense that one of ten years' standing incurs, but not one of less than ten years' standing;
there is an offense that one of less than ten years' standing incurs, but not one of ten years' standing.
There is an offense that both one who has ten years of seniority and one who has less than ten years commit.
There is an offense that one who has five years commits, but not one who has less than five;
there is an offense that one who has less than five years commits, but not one who has five years.
There is an offense that one commits both when having five years of seniority and when having less than five years of seniority.
There is an offense that one commits with a wholesome mind;
there is an offense that one commits with an unwholesome mind.
There is an offense that one commits with an indeterminate mind.
There is an offense that one commits while experiencing pleasant feeling;
there is an offense that one commits while experiencing painful feeling.
There is an offense that one who experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling commits.
There are three grounds for censure:
what has been seen, what has been heard, and suspicion.
There are three ways of taking voting tickets:
secretly, openly, and whispering into the ear.
There are three kinds of refusals:
Great desire, lack of contentment, and lack of austerity.
Three are permitted:
fewness of wishes, contentment, and austerity.
There are also three things that are rejected:
great desire, lack of contentment, and lack of moderation.
Three things are permitted:
Fewness of wishes, contentment, and moderation.
Three types of formulations:
a formulation, a subsequent formulation, and an unarisen formulation.
There are also three other types of designation:
universal designation, partial designation, and common designation.
There are also another three types of designation:
There is designation by what is not common, designation from one side, and designation from both sides.
There is an offense that a fool commits, but not a wise person;
there is an offense that a wise person commits, but not a fool.
There is an offense that both a fool and a wise person commit.
There is an offense committed during the dark fortnight, but not during the bright fortnight;
there is an offense committed during the bright fortnight, but not during the dark fortnight.
There is an offense that one commits both during the dark fortnight and during the bright fortnight.
There is that which is allowable during the dark fortnight but not during the bright fortnight; there is that which is allowable during the bright fortnight but not during the dark fortnight.
There is that which is allowable both during the dark fortnight and during the bright fortnight.
There is an offense one commits in winter, but not in summer or the rainy season;
there is an offense one commits in summer, but not in winter or the rainy season.
There is an offense that one commits in the rainy season, but not in the winter, nor in the summer.
There is an offense that the Saṅgha commits, but neither a group nor an individual.
There is an offense that a group commits, but neither the Saṅgha nor an individual.
There is an offense that an individual commits, but neither the Saṅgha nor a group does.
There is what is allowable for the Saṅgha, but not for a group or an individual;
there is what is allowable for a group, but not for the Saṅgha or an individual.
There is that which is allowable for an individual, but not for a Saṅgha, nor for a Gaṇa.
There are three kinds of concealment:
one conceals the matter, but not the offense.
One conceals the offense but not the matter;
one conceals both the matter and the offense.
There are three ways of concealing:
A sauna-shelter, a water-shelter, and a clothing-shelter.
Three things move when covered, not when uncovered:
a woman moves when covered, not when uncovered.
The mantras of the brahmins proceed in secrecy, not openly;
wrong view proceeds in secrecy, not openly.
Three things shine when they are open, not when they are secret: [the sun, the moon, and the Dhamma].
The lunar disk shines when it is uncovered, not when it is covered;
the solar disk shines when it is uncovered, not when it is covered;
the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata shines when it is uncovered, not when it is covered.
There are three ways of taking lodgings:
the first, the last, and the intermediate release.
There is an offense for one who is ill, not for one who is not ill.
There is an offense that one who is not ill incurs, but one who is ill does not;
there is an offense that both one who is ill and one who is not ill incur.
There are three ways of suspending the Pātimokkha that are illegitimate.
There are three lawful suspensions of the Pātimokkha.
There are three types of probation:
probation for concealed offenses, probation for unconcealed offenses, and probation for the end of purity.
There are three types of *mānatta* penance:
*mānatta* for concealed offenses, *mānatta* for unconcealed offenses, and *mānatta* for the fortnight.
There are three ways in which the night-count of a monk undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*) is broken:
Living together, living apart, and failure to inform.
There is an offense committed inside, not outside;
there is an offense committed outside, not inside.
There is an offense that one incurs both within and without.
There is an offense that one incurs within the boundary, not outside the boundary;
there is an offense that one incurs outside the boundary, not within the boundary.
There is an offense that one commits both within the boundary and outside the boundary.
One commits an offense in three ways:
by means of the body, by means of speech, or by means of both body and speech.
One commits an offense in three ways:
in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, or in the presence of an individual.
One emerges from an offense in three ways:
One emerges from the offense by means of the body, by means of speech, or by means of both body and speech.
Furthermore, one emerges from the offense in three ways:
in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, or in the presence of an individual.
There are three illegitimate ways of granting *amūḷhavinaya*.
There are three legitimate ways of granting *amūḷhavinaya*.
If a monk possesses three qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a censure transaction (*tajjanīyakamma*) against him.

He is one who creates quarrels, creates strife, creates disputes, creates contention, and creates legal issues in the Saṅgha; he is foolish and incompetent, full of offenses and unrestrained, and he dwells in association with householders through improper associations with householders.

When a bhikkhu possesses these three factors—the fact that he creates quarrels … [as above] … and creates legal issues in the Saṅgha, that he is foolish and incompetent, full of offenses and unrestrained, and that he dwells in association with householders through improper associations with householders—the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of demotion against him.
If the Saṅgha so desires, it may carry out a formal act of banishment against a bhikkhu who possesses three qualities:

he is a quarrelsome maker of strife … [as above] … he is a creator of legal disputes in the Saṅgha; he is ignorant and incompetent; he is full of offenses and lacks remorse; he is a defiler of families and of evil conduct, and his evil conduct is both seen and heard.
If the Saṅgha so desires, it may carry out a formal act of reconciliation against a bhikkhu who possesses three qualities: [the same as above].

He is a quarrelsome person … [as above] … he causes legal disputes in the Saṅgha; he is foolish and incompetent; he is full of offenses and has not relinquished them; he reviles and abuses householders.
When a bhikkhu possesses these three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense against him:

he is a quarrelsome person … [as above] … he causes legal disputes in the Saṅgha; he is foolish and incompetent; he is full of offenses and has not relinquished them; having committed an offense, he does not wish to see that offense.
If a monk possesses three qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for refusal to make amends for an offense:

he is a creator of strife … [as above] … he is a creator of legal issues in the Saṅgha; he is ignorant and incompetent; he is full of offenses and lacks self-restraint, and having committed an offense, he does not wish to make amends for that offense.
If a monk possesses three qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for refusal to relinquish an evil view: [the same three qualities as above].

He is a maker of quarrels... [as above] ...a maker of legal issues in the Saṅgha; he is foolish and incompetent, full of offenses, and without purification; he does not wish to relinquish an evil view.
When a monk possesses three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may impose a severe penalty upon him:

he is a maker of quarrels, a maker of strife, a maker of disputes, a maker of contention, and a maker of legal issues in the Saṅgha; he is foolish and incompetent, full of offenses, and without purification; he dwells in association with householders through improper associations with householders.
A legal procedure may be carried out against a bhikkhu who possesses three qualities:
he is shameless, he is ignorant, and he is unassimilated to the Teaching.
A legal procedure may also be carried out against a bhikkhu who possesses another three qualities: [he is shameless, he is ignorant, and he is unassimilated to the Teaching].
He is failed in virtue regarding higher virtue; he is failed in conduct regarding higher conduct; he is failed in view regarding higher view.
Furthermore, a formal act (kamma) should be performed against a bhikkhu who possesses three other factors:
he is possessed of bodily frivolity, he is possessed of verbal frivolity, and he is possessed of both bodily and verbal frivolity.
A formal act should also be performed against a bhikkhu who possesses another three factors:
